emails.subject: Clinical Trial Opportunity For Long Term Anti Thyroid Drug Users
emails.content:
A Trial to Assess IMVT-1402 As a Treatment For Graves Disease

This week, I came across a clinical trial in the 2B phase of research. This means that they are testing IMVT-1402 on a larger sample population, and further testing the efficacy, safety, and tolerability in adult Graves Disease patients, who are actively hyperthyroid despite anti-thyroid drug treatment.

What is IMVT-1402?

IMVT-1402 is a fully human, monoclonal antibody in clinical development as a potential treatment for a variety of immunoglobulin G (IgG)-mediated autoimmune diseases. It is an investigational drug being developed by an immunology company called Immunovant.

It is being investigated for a variety of autoimmune diseases, such as Graves' Disease, Myasthenia Gravis, and Difficult-to-treat Rheumatoid Arthritis.

How Phase 2A Performed

https://www.clinicaltrialsarena.com/news/immunovant-touts-positive-phase-ii-batoclimab-data-as-imvt-1402-also-progresses/?cf-view

IMVT-1402 is the next generation of Batoclimab, which was specifically designed to address a safety issue, which was an increase in overall cholesterol, observed in Batoclimab.

The 2A proof of concept trial was promising. The study ran long term Graves Disease patients, of whom do not respond well to anti-thyroid drugs. weeks, 56% of patients were able to completely stop taking anti-thyroid drugs. Of the patients, 80% were female, their median age years, and their median time since Graves’ disease diagnosis .7 months. There were no deaths reported from this trial.

It was also seen to have improved Graves Eye Disease symptoms.

More About This Trial

This upcoming clinical trial will be much longer, years in total. There will be a split into screening, treatment, and assessment periods. Immunovant will also be assessing how long patients are able to stay off of anti thyroid drugs after receiving the medication.

There are also many clear pros and cons of joining a clinical trial like this:

Pros and Cons of Participating

Pros

Cons

An opportunity to receive a novel treatment if you are not interested in radioactive iodine or surgery, and anti thyroid drugs do not work for you.


Directly contribute to medical research and science for Graves Disease.


Financial benefit of receiving this treatment for free, when it may become very expensive in the future (with no guarantee of being fully covered by insurance).

Inconvenience. It’s a very long trial, with weekly injections over the span of a year. Each injection could take over an hour (to monitor for potential side effects). It will also likely be during business hours, depending on your chosen location.


Limited trial locations, many primarily in the USA.


Potential unknown side effects that may effect you in the future.


Possibility of a placebo. There is % chance of receiving a placebo for this study, and neither you nor the researchers will know.


You may not receive any other forms of treatment other than anti thyroid drugs throughout the course of this study. This includes any treatment for Graves Eye Disease. (However, you may leave at any time.)

You can access more information about this clinical trial on this website: https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT06727604#study-overview

You may also sign up here: https://graves.clinicalenrollment.com/

What does this mean for you?

It’s very exciting to see that there is actively enrolling medical research related to Graves Disease, for those of us unable to normalize using anti-thyroid drugs. It also gives some relief to those who may be in remission currently, but concerned about staying in this state. It is largely up to each individual if they would be interested in such a trial, and it is a big commitment.

I personally have decided to try this study, and will update with any new news I find while participating. Thanks for reading!

emails.subject: The Future of Graves' Disease Treatment Could Look Different
emails.content:
How Graves Treatment May Shift to More Autoimmune Focus

Happy New Year!

A few weeks ago, I had the privilege of attending a conference hosted by the Canadian Society of Endocrinology and Metabolism.

During this conference, I met endocrinologists, nurse practitioners, researchers, and pharmaceutical reps for drugs like Tepezza.

I also learned a lot about thyroid disease and thyroid cancer! I’d love to share some of what I learned, and some other information I found related to how thyroid disease treatment may evolve in the future.

History of Graves Disease Treatment

In the past, the most popular treatment choice for hyperthyroidism was radioactive iodine. In 2011, a survey of endocrinologists found that % utilized radioactive iodine for their patients. In a recent 2023 survey of 1252 endocrinologists, .5% of respondents said that they preferred anti-thyroid drugs (ATDs).

Thus, the trend towards anti-thyroid drugs has been significant in the past decade.

Improvements

There has been many fascinating studies published that show a real improvement in Graves Disease treatment. Experimental drugs, mostly biologics, as well as reliance on technical wearable devices has become more apparent.

Batoclimab

https://www.medscape.com/viewarticle/batoclimab-shows-rapid-...

A recent study (November 2024) utilized a drug called Batoclimab to reduce key Graves’ Disease markers, such as TRaB. Batoclimab is an an investigational, fully human monoclonal antibody that is currently in the clinical investigation phase.

So far, the study has ran long term Graves Disease patients, of whom do not respond well to anti-thyroid drugs. They saw a normalization of serum free thyroxine (T4) weeks of administration of the drug, and free triiodothyronine (T3) and T4 remained normal within the higher upper limit of normal until . Of the patients, 80% were female, their median age years, and their median time since Graves’ disease diagnosis .7 months.

Also, it had positive improvements on cardiovascular, eye, and anxiety symptoms.

Overall, this study had positive results! More importantly, it is focused on targeting the underlying autoimmune root cause, rather than just hormone levels. However, it’s very important to note that this was a small, early phase trial with no placebo or control group. So it’s difficult to know what could have been just natural disease progression, versus actual influence from the drug itself.

TSH Receptor Disruption Drug

https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/35088429/

Another drug called K1-70 was evaluated during a Trial. K1-70 is a a promising human monoclonal antibody that functions by blocking the thyroid-stimulating hormone receptor (TSHR) that causes the overactive thyroid.

During the study, 18 Graves Disease patients were given varying dosage levels of K1-70. During this trial, they found that TSH levels were able to rise significantly, while T3 and T4 levels decreased. Patients were either in the euthyroid or hypothyroid state.

Wearable Devices

Tracking your health using wearable devices may give you the right data to ask for earlier tests in the doctor’s office. Many endocrinologists can use markers such as changes in heart rate to decide whether an earlier test may be necessary.

What does this mean for you?

This is a really hopeful time in which it is clear that the use of human biologics could potentially make treatment of Graves Disease faster than ever. It’s also clear that there is a shift in treating it more like an autoimmune condition, rather than a thyroid condition. We will have to wait and see if new phases of these trials come out, and how they could potentially affect things like remission rates and long term improvements.

In addition, it’s clear that it’s more important than ever for patients to advocate for our own health. The use of technology to track crucial Graves related symptoms, such as heart rate, can really help with getting faster treatment plans.

emails.content:
I'm going to an endocrinology conference!


...and I want to get your questions answered! Find out more and how to submit questions below.

Next week, I have the privilege of attending the Diabetes Canada and Canadian Society of Endocrinology and Metabolism (CSEM) Professional Conference. It is the most highly anticipated endocrinology-related conference in Canada to learn about significant advances in research, treatment and care. It is an entire conference filled with endocrinologists who are at the top of their field.

Do you have a burning question?

If there is a question you really want answered that is never being answered in clinics, please submit them by joining our Discord or Facebook group, and submitting a chat or post.

I will gather the most frequently asked questions, and either record the answers through text QnA style, or actually record doctors giving their answers (depending on the guidelines of recording at the event, and individual doctors comfort).

Click the images below, or the following links:

Discord: https://discord.gg/U74fDNKwuM

Facebook: https://www.facebook.com/share/g/1ANJdCzvL2/

Guidelines of what to ask

Unfortunately, I cannot get any specific medical advice answered. 

❌ Please do not ask for the following:

  • Personal medical advice
  • Diagnostic questions
  • Urgent or emergency concerns
  • Questions requiring images or lab reports 
✅ Please do ask the hard hitting questions! Some examples:
  • How do you explain flare ups to patients? 
  • Why is Graves Disease treated as more of a thyroid problem than a autoimmune problem?
  • What do you feel patients are not the best at doing when getting treated for this condition?


Thanks for reading! I look forward to reading your questions, and sharing answers next week.

emails.subject: Selenium: Separating Fact from Fiction
emails.content:
Selenium: Separating Fact from Fiction

There is a lot of information out there about supplements. However, it’s a widely unregulated industry with tons of misinformation. So, I wanted to break down some studies related to selenium and Graves Disease. Also, a bit about geography, where selenium even comes from, and selenium supplements versus Brazil nuts.

What is Selenium?

Selenium is a trace mineral essential for antioxidant defense, immune function, and thyroid hormone production. It is extremely crucial to your health, and your body can’t produce it on it’s own. Thus, the only way to get it is through your diet.

Brazil nuts is a common dietary food to get the daily fill of selenium (55 mg for adults). However, selenium also comes from protein sources such as seafood, meat (especially organ meats), eggs, and poultry.

Graves Eye Disease and Selenium (trial)

https://www.nejm.org/doi/10.1056/NEJMoa1012985?url_ver=Z39.88-2003&rfr_id=ori:rid:crossref.org&rfr_dat=cr_pub 0www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov

A trial was run on 159 [mild] Graves Eye Disease patients months to assess the efficacy of selenium on the disease. Of the 159 patients, 54 received twice-daily doses of selenium supplements (100 mcg per dose). They were given this dosage for the months, and then it was stopped for months afterwards. This trial was run in Europe.

Selenium administration significantly improved quality of life and slowed progression of the disease in patients with mild Graves' eye disease. It is also possible that selenium may have beneficial effects in moderate-to-severe Graves Eye Disease, especially when patients are selenium-deficient. Although, this was not proven in this trial.

Selenium and Graves Disease as a Whole

However, when we consider Graves Disease as whole, the research gets a bit confusing. There has been some studies that say that Graves Disease thyroid levels were improved, and helped patients stay in a euthyroid state. A notable study that backs this statement was run in Croatia, a selenium deficient country, when patients of Graves Disease were given selenium supplements in addition to methimazole over a span days. The selenium seemed to improve patient outcomes in a real way.

However, other studies that have been run in countries without selenium deficiency (namely the US) prove that selenium made little to no impact on the outcome of Graves Disease.

But am I already getting it from my diet?

Now, this is a very important question when considering selenium supplementation. Selenium deficiency affects about 15% of the world globally.

Since selenium comes from the soil, and is then transferred to us via protein in our diet, but it is highly dependent on the area that you are living in.

Some areas that have a history of being deficient in selenium include:

  1. Europe - particularly Eastern Europe
  2. United Kingdom
  3. Parts of China
  4. Ethiopia
  5. Malawi
  6. New Zealand

Areas that are proven to not be deficient in selenium:

  1. United States
  2. Canada

Selenium supplements versus Brazil Nuts

Brazil Nuts are a supplement heavy food that can easily give you your daily dosage of selenium with -2 nuts. Another option to get selenium is to take selenium supplements. A recent study in New Zealand studied the difference in selenium levels for patients who took two brazil nuts, or 100 mg of selenium supplementation over week period. They found that in the brazil nuts group, levels were raised %, while the selenium supplement group was raised %. Thus, Brazil Nuts were just as effective in raising selenium levels as supplements.

Thus, it’s clear that it is largely up to personal preference of which is better. The only main concern with Brazil Nuts is the potential to take too much selenium if the patient were to take more -2 brazil nuts per day. If you were to take more -2 brazil nuts a day, it could potentially lead to an selenium toxicity, which can also be harmful to health.

What does this mean for you?

The decision to take selenium supplements is largely up to personal preference, as there isn’t a strong case linking it to a better Graves outcome. However, if you live in an area known for selenium deficiency, or have Graves Eye Disease, there are proven links between selenium supplements and better health outcomes.


Thanks for reading! Tune in next week for more Graves research 🙂

emails.subject: The Power of Strength Training On Your Thyroid Health
emails.content:
The Power of Strength Training On Thyroid Health

Initially, I was planning on sharing all the ways that the thyroid can be linked to poor bone health, Osteoporosis, and all of the potential risks that can come with that. However, I found an amazing trial (called the LIFTMOR trial) that completely renewed my hope for my future, and made me recognize that there may be some semblance of control over this disease with lifestyle changes. I hope after reading this newsletter, you’ll find some renewed hope as well.

But first, let me introduce why you should care about your bones. 🦴

﻿Everything is always connected

﻿﻿﻿In a normal body, when a bone experiences mechanical stress (typically from exercise such as running, walking, etc.) the bone remodelling process is triggered. This is the continuous process where old bone tissue is replaced by new bone tissue. It helps maintain bone strength and regulate calcium in the body. It’s also broken up key [overlapping] steps: Activation, Resorption, Reversal, Formation, and Termination, happening over a span of -6 months.

However, with hyperthyroidism, the body more frequently initiates the bone remodelling process, combined with the fact that there is an imbalance between the Resorption and Formation phases. This causes a net loss of % of bone per remodelling cycle.

﻿﻿This loss causes patients with active hyperthyroidism to be at higher risk of contracting Osteoporosis, which is a condition in which the bones become weak and brittle, making them more susceptible to fractures.

﻿﻿﻿What the LIFTMOR Trial Reveals

﻿﻿﻿https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1002/jbmr.3284﻿﻿

The LIFTMOR Trial was a trial run on 101 post menopausal women, 58 years or older, who were diagnosed with Osteopenia and Osteoporosis.

It was run months, in participants -minute, twice weekly, supervised high-intensity, progressive resistance and impact weight-bearing training (HIRIT). Their exercises included varying weights and forms of exercise, including squats and deadlifts. They also had a control group participants who did low intensity home based exercise. They aimed to monitor and determine the efficacy of high resistance training for people with low bone density.

Amazingly, they discovered that the high resistance group improved in almost all physical activity measurements, with zero fractures.

These included leg and back strength, ability to sit to stand in a reasonable amount of time, vertical jump, and functional reach. The improvements for the high resistance groups was % in terms of back and leg strength, 11% in terms of sit to stand time, % in terms of vertical jump and functional reach. Comparatively for the control group, who only saw -10% improvement in back and leg strength, a -2% worsening in sit to stand time, and no changes in vertical jump and functional reach.

Their conclusion was that HiRIT exercise intervention was efficacious and superior to previous programs for enhancing bone at clinically relevant sites, as well as stature and functional performance of relevance to falls in postmenopausal women.

What does it mean for you?

This trial tells us an important thing about illness: Our condition cannot stop us from improving our health.

These women had low bone density, were above the age , and already had a preexisting condition of Osteoporosis or Osteopenia. By all previously known logic, high resistance training could have been disastrous for them! But with the help of their supervisor/trainer, and potentially renewed hope from the trial, they were able to drastically improve their strength by %.

This shows us that our condition cannot stop us from improving our health. Although hyperthyroidism causes a myriad of antagonizing mental health symptoms, any day you can overcome and take a step to improving your health will be worth it.

On a more practical level, since hyperthyroid patients are at a higher risk of contracting Osteoporosis, you could also potentially help with prevention.

It is important to note that availability and feasibility of high resistance training may not be the same for everyone. Of course, finding a skilled trainer to help you is not cheap. Also, there were many people who were not eligible for this study, most importantly including those who have conditions that cannot participate in high intensity exercise. Thus, it is always responsible to talk to your doctor/endocrinologist before ever trying something new.

But if you can make this investment into supervised strength training, it may be one of the best quality of life investments you could make.

Thanks for reading! Tune in next week to see more interesting topics about thyroid research.

emails.subject: How your thyroid may be changing your brain
emails.content:
I think it’s fairly common to hear that psychological symptoms, such as anxiety, depression, and mental fatigue, are the hardest to be taken seriously in a doctors office. Especially for women, it’s fairly common that we hear that these symptoms are unrelated to the disease, and are more of a “grey area” in terms of symptoms. Or, even more common, we don’t mention them at all.

Is it all about the numbers?

Graves disease is an autoimmune condition that manifests when the body attacks itself and in turn, produces too much thyroid hormone. This overproduction of thyroid hormone is known as hyperthyroidism. In order to better control the disease, clinicians treat the underlying hyperthyroidism with anti-thyroid drugs, surgery, or radioactive iodine.

However, since it is an autoimmune condition, there can be other parts of the body that it can affect, other than just the thyroid. Some commonly known victims are the eyes and skin. In the last few years, there has been research into how the brain could potentially be affected by Graves Disease and hyperthyroidism.

﻿﻿The Studies

There have been two main studies I have found regarding structural brain changes caused by hyperthyroidism.

Research on processing speed, attention, and emotional expression

﻿This study was published by a group in Sweden in 2022, which premenopausal women with recently diagnosed Graves Disease. They aimed to to investigate how hyperthyroidism affects the brain, particularly regions involved in emotion, attention, and memory. Of women in the study, % were treated with anti-thyroid medication, 33% we’re treated with a total surgical removal of their thyroid patient was treated with radioactive iodine.

Over a span months, they regularly tested the study participants thyroid levels, and took objective brain measurements, assessing cognitive/attention tasks.

Through their study, they we’re able to find that there was a significant amount of reduced grey matter volume. This finding implies that it can cause impaired memory and cognitive function. Although it could not be linked to symptom severity, it shows that Graves Disease actually had real consequence on the brain for a large majority of the participants.

However, upon treatment of the condition, it was clear that the brain matter was able to return to normal, and there was little to no permanent damage on the brain. Although, it was found that symptomatic recovery was not linked to increase in brain volumes.

Research on your brains "moderator"

This study was published by a research group in 2018, which patients with recently diagnosed Graves Disease. They aimed to to investigate how hyperthyroidism affects the brain, particularly regions involved in memory and context switching. They studied a portion of the brain, called the salience network (SN). This part of your brain is primarily responsible for detecting important stimuli, and directing attention. They tested patients thyroid levels, as well as fMRI to reach their results.

After a month of anti-thyroid medication, they patients fMRI. Through their findings, they found that when thyroid hormones become unbalanced, it temporarily disrupted how certain brain networks communicate, especially those involved in focus and attention. It affected the way the saliance network was able to direct important stimuli. After about a month of treatment, this communication begins to improve.

However, some unusual patterns of brain activity remain even after treatment. These lasting changes may be the brain’s way of trying to compensate for the emotional and thinking problems caused by the disease.

What does it mean for you?

Although the results are not super conclusive on what part of thyroid autoimmunity is actually causing these brain changes (other than changes in thyroid hormone), it gives us a clear understanding of why things like attention, emotions, and memory are so hard to maintain while we are ill. It also gives a real grasp on what is going on inside our bodies while these symptoms are occurring.
